newsitem.title: FRANCE: Striking French truckers, bosses in new talks.
newsitem.headline: Striking French truckers, bosses in new talks.

text.p: French truckers' leaders and employers were locked in new marathon talks on Wednesday as truckers kept up barricades on roads that are starting to throttle the economy.

Wednesday will also test wider union disaffection in France. The big Communist-led CGT union is urging workers to rally at the truckers' barricades to express support and step up pressure on Prime Minister Alain Juppe to drop austerity policies.

Truckers and haulage bosses, meeting in an annex of the Transport Ministry in Paris as the strikes entered a 10th day, were debating strikers' demands for higher pay, shorter hours and retirement at 55 instead of 60.

The strikers have set up almost 200 truck blocakdes on major routes and blocked refineries and fuel depots around France, closing some petrol stations, forcing factory closures and squeezing supplies of goods like fruit or fish.
The strike, the most serious labour unrest in France this year, is also starting to disrupt mail, grain imports and angering foreign truckers blocked on French roads.
Some regions have started to ration sales of fuel to motorists, keeping supplies for fire engines and ambulances.

The talks under way on Wednesday's began at 3 p.m. (1400 GMT) on Tuesday, the third consecutive overnight session. Media reports said one proposal under discussion was a compromise on retirement at 57-1/2, largely funded by the state.

Police were deployed around the Transport Ministry after a call by three taxi drivers' unions to "join the truckers" and demonstrate for their own demands. Half a dozen taxis turned up early on Wednesday.

The French franc stayed under pressure at around 3.3925 per mark. Traders said markets feared the strike could spread, or that the government would agree to the strikers' demands and encourage costly copycat strikes in other sectors.

CGT union boss Louis Viannet planned to meet striking truckers at Saint-Pol-de-Mer in northern France near a blocked refinery to show his support for their movement. The CGT wants Wednesday to be a national day of action and rallies.

And the Force Ouvriere union, which led a 24-day wave of anti-government strikes with the CGT that virtually paralysed France in late 1995, has also said it is considering widening the strikes to public transport.
Transport problems will widen on Wednesday with the first day of a two-day strike by pilots, stewards and engineers on French airlines protesting against feared job cuts and restructurings.
State airline Air France said it would guarantee two-thirds of long-haul flights and just a quarter of medium-haul flights.

The airline's short-haul unit Air France Europe, which operates mainly domestic routes, expected to cut more than half its flights. It said it would guarantee 213 flights on Wednesday and 200 on Thursday, against 480 normally each day.
On the railways, three unions were staging a 24-hour strike from Tuesday evening at the Sotteville-les-Rouen depot in northwest France, a symbolic bastion during last year's strikes.
The south and west of the country, including the city of Bordeaux where Juppe is mayor, have been hardest hit although the actions are slowly extending to other regions.
On Tuesday night, truckers widened their actions to block access to an oil depot on the Rhine in Strasbourg, eastern France, and the Reichstett refinery.

On Tuesday, truckers sealed off a petrol depot at Grigny which supplies 90 percent of petrol sold in hypermarkets in the Paris region. Food industry sources said 70 to 80 percent of food supplies had gone through so far, but shortages may begin if the protests go into next week.
